
❯ write a 300 word story about a lighthouse keeper, no tools, just prose

⏺ The light failed twice that winter. Both times Aldous Renn climbed the hundred and ninety steps carrying a hand lamp,
  as though shaming the great lens with a smaller flame might embarrass it back into service.

  He was sixty-one and had kept the Fennwick light for twenty-three years. He knew its moods the way a farrier knows a
  horse: the shudder in the gearing when the wind came hard off the northwest, the particular whine the clockwork made
  in cold that meant the weights wanted regreasing. The Board sent inspectors every spring. They wrote in their ledgers
  that the station was in good order and never once asked him how he knew when the fog was coming, which was by the ache
  behind his left ear, four hours out, reliable as a barometer.

  His wife had died in the second year. People assumed the isolation was a wound he was nursing. It was not. The truth,
  which he never told anyone because it sounded unkind, was that he liked the arrangement of his days. Wick trimmed at
  four. Brass polished Tuesdays. The log filled in his small upright hand: wind, visibility, vessels sighted. There was
  no argument in it. The sea asked one thing of him and he gave it, and in return nothing else was required.

  In March a trawler went down on the Barrow shoals in weather he had signaled clean. He walked the beach for six days.
  He found a glove, a crate lid, and a boy's boot, and he wrote all three in the log because the log was for what
  happened, not for what he wished had happened.

  The Board retired him in the autumn. He took a cottage two miles inland, well out of sight of the water, and every
  night at dusk he stood at the back door and listened for the horn.

✻ Churned for 17s

❯ write a 250 word essay about tide pools, prose only, no tools

⏺ A tide pool is a lease, not a home. Twice a day the ocean withdraws and leaves behind a basin of water that is, for
  the next six hours, a small closed world running an experiment on its inhabitants. The temperature climbs. Salinity
  rises as water evaporates, then crashes when rain falls. Oxygen drops through the afternoon. Nothing living there is
  comfortable; everything living there is specialized.
